title: Water a house plant at its roots without wetting its leaves
instruction: Water the plant at its roots, onto the soil, without wetting its leaves. Then put the jug back on its stool, leave the plant's leaves as they were and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Many house plants (and seedlings, and vegetables in a bed) must be watered at the soil, not over the leaves, which rot or scorch when wet; with leaves spread over the pot, one hand holds the foliage aside while the other pours, as in caring for plants at home, in a nursery or in a care home.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A terracotta pot 17 cm across and 7.5 cm tall on a saucer, its middle 30 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, filled with dark soil 1.3 cm below its rim; fixed. In it a house plant with a green stem and broad leaves (15 cm long, up to 13 cm wide) spread low over the soil: three fixed in the crown, over the back and both sides of the pot, and one big leaf in front on a springy stalk, joined to the stem 10 cm above the table, lying over the front of the soil and reaching out 6 cm past the rim toward the arms. Pushed round on its stalk, the big leaf springs back over the soil when let go. (2) A blue plastic watering jug (5.4 cm across, 8.5 cm tall, with a pouring lip and a handle) holding 120 ml of water, simulated as 12 drops (7 mm beads, 10 ml each), standing on a beech stool 6 cm tall, 26 cm forward and 13 cm left of the centre line. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: an ordinary artificial house plant (an artificial peace lily, say) with moulded green plastic leaves, which take up no water, 15 cm long and up to 13 cm wide, set as above: three in the crown over the back and sides of the pot, and the big lower leaf on a sprung wire stalk lying over the front of the soil, which springs back when let go. Each leaf is fixed to its wire stalk with a small clip, so it can be unclipped for the weighings and photographs. Before each trial both faces of every leaf get a dried blue film of butterfly pea flower extract, a natural pH indicator that turns pink or purple wherever an acid touches it (see scoring). The plant stands in real potting soil, just moist, in the same 17 cm glazed terracotta pot on its saucer, with the drainage hole plugged by a rubber bung for the trial. The jug (about 150 ml) holds 120 ml of room-temperature dilute white vinegar as the water (1 part ordinary 5% white vinegar to 9 parts water: about 0.5% acetic acid, pH about 2.9). It is 99.5% water, so it pours and weighs as water does, and on plastic leaves it harms nothing. Two cameras film the trial at 60 frames a second, overhead and from the side, as supporting evidence only.
scoring: Judged at the end. Real trial: (a) liquid delivered to the soil is weighed (the dilute vinegar weighs as water does: 1 g = 1 ml). The pot is weighed in the same state before and after, with its four plastic leaves unclipped (it keeps its soil, stem, wire stalks, clips and bung). Before the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out of its saucer and weigh it, and the dry saucer, on a kitchen scale (1 g steps), then clip the leaves back on; after the trial, unclip the leaves (below), lift the pot out, let it drip into the saucer, and weigh the pot and the saucer. The pot's gain is the liquid delivered to the soil (its drainage hole is plugged, and the 1.3 cm of headroom above the soil holds about 235 ml, so none leaves the pot); the saucer's gain is spilled liquid and never counts as delivered. (b) leaf contact is a chemical record, not a view. Liquid A: 2 g of dried butterfly pea flowers steeped about 10 minutes in 100 ml of water just off the boil, cooled and filtered through a paper coffee filter. While unclipped before the trial, each leaf, wiped clean and dry, is sprayed on both faces from a fine-mist bottle in light coats, each left to dry, until a uniform blue film forms, then photographed on both faces against a white card. Liquid B, in the jug: 12 ml of ordinary 5% white vinegar and 108 ml of water (about 0.5% acetic acid, pH about 2.9). Wherever B touches the film, however briefly, at an edge, as a drop running off, or out of the cameras' view behind the jug or a gripper, the film turns pink or purple, and the mark stays once dry. After the trial each leaf is unclipped by its clip in clean dry gloves (skin is mildly acidic), laid on a white card, left until dry and photographed on both faces in the same light. Any pink or purple spot or streak on any leaf that is not in its before photo is leaf contact. The videos are supporting evidence only. Simulation: each of the 12 beads stands for 10 ml. A bead is leaf contact if it ever touches a leaf or comes within 4 mm of one (a margin for the splash and spread a rigid bead lacks), checked after every physics step (240 times a second); it counts as delivered only if it ends lying on the soil inside the pot's wall (its centre within 7.25 cm of the pot's axis and between 3 mm below and 15 mm above the soil's surface) without ever having touched a leaf. Beads that miss the pot, bounce out of it or land in the saucer never count. Both record the same event, any liquid contact with a leaf, which breaks the instruction's constraint: 0.0 if any bead ever touched a leaf (in a real trial, any pink or purple mark). Otherwise 1.0: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads), the jug back on its stool (within 3 cm, upright within 15 degrees), the big leaf back over the soil (within 12 degrees of where it lay), both hands let go (each TCP at least 4 cm from the jug and the leaf) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm); in a real trial the end state is checked against marks on the stool and the pot's rim (ruler and protractor) and the robot's joint log. 0.5: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads), without the end state. 0.25: at least 40 ml delivered (pot gain at least 40 g; 4 beads). Else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the jug, the big leaf and every bead still.
reset_notes: Pull the bung and let the pot drain, then plug it again (it is weighed afresh, leaves unclipped, before each trial); empty, rinse and dry the saucer; rinse the film off the plastic leaves, dry them, coat and photograph them afresh with liquid A (see scoring) and clip them back on; lay the big leaf back over the soil; refill the jug with 120 ml of liquid B (the dilute vinegar), dry its outside and stand it on its stool.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control). Simplified: 120 ml of water is 12 rigid 7 mm beads (10 ml each, 0.8 g) that do not cling or splash; a bead touching or within 4 mm of a leaf is leaf contact (in real trials, dilute vinegar marks a pH-indicator film on the leaves pink). The saucer is drawn only. Leaves are rigid plates (plastic in real trials); the crown's leaves and the pot are fixed, and the big leaf turns on its stalk against a spring (0.0016 N m per degree).
